title: Influences of culture and environmental attitude on thermal, emotional and perceptual evaluations of a public square
central_proposition: Thermal, emotional, and perceptual assessments of a public square are significantly influenced by cultural background and environmental attitude, even under objectively similar comfortable thermal conditions, suggesting that psychological schema-based and socio-cultural processes intertwine with physical environmental factors.

concept_definitions.name: Culture
concept_definitions.definition: The system of information that codes the manner in which people in an organized group, society or nation interact with their social and physical environment.

concept_definitions.name: Schemata
concept_definitions.definition: Sets of knowledge structures and expectations stored in memory that may elicit behavioural, affective and cognitive consequences.

concept_definitions.name: Environmental attitude (urban vs open-air person)
concept_definitions.definition: Participants' self-identification on a 5-point Likert scale (1=mostly urban, 5=mostly open-air) based on pleasure in street life/shops vs. sea/woods/nature.

concept_definitions.name: Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET)
concept_definitions.definition: The air temperature at which the energy balance for assumed indoor conditions is balanced with the same mean skin temperature and sweat rate as calculated for the actual outdoor conditions.

argument_structure: The paper first reviews limitations of existing thermal comfort indices in outdoor and cross-cultural contexts. It then proposes that psychological processes (schemata, attitudes) and cultural factors mediate environmental perception. A quasi-experimental study compares Swedish and Japanese participants' thermal, emotional, and perceptual assessments of public squares under similar PET conditions. The findings demonstrate significant cultural and attitude-based differences, supporting the hypothesis that subjective evaluations are intertwined with psychological and socio-cultural processes beyond objective physical parameters.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The proposed mechanism is that individuals' perceptions and evaluations of the environment, including thermal comfort, emotions, and aesthetics, are not solely determined by objective physical parameters (like PET). Instead, these perceptions are filtered and interpreted through psychological schema-based processes (prior knowledge, expectations) and socio-cultural processes (cultural norms, learned attitudes, 'cultural response bias'). These internal and cultural lenses lead to divergent subjective experiences even when objective environmental conditions are similar.

findings.mechanism: Cultural priors/schemata influencing thermal perception, leading Japanese participants to estimate weather as warmer and feel less comfortable despite similar objective thermal conditions.
findings.quote: Japanese participants estimated the current weather as warmer than did Swedish participants and, consistent with this, they felt less thermally comfortable on the site

findings.consequent: Perceived weather (windier, colder), Perceived site (windier, colder)
findings.mechanism: Cultural priors/schemata influencing weather perception, leading Swedish participants to estimate weather and site as windier and colder.
findings.quote: Compared to the Japanese, the Swedes estimated both the current weather and the site as windier and colder, indicating a consistency in weather assessment

findings.consequent: Emotional state (more glad, calm), Perceived aesthetics (more beautiful, pleasant)
findings.mechanism: Cultural character/schemata influencing emotional and aesthetic evaluations of the place.
findings.quote: Swedish participants felt more glad and calm on the site and, in line with their character (more glad than gloomy), they estimated the square as more beautiful and pleasant

findings.consequent: Thermal, emotional, and perceptual assessments of a physical place
findings.mechanism: These processes filter and interpret objective environmental stimuli, leading to subjective evaluations that diverge from purely physiological predictions.
findings.quote: All this indicates that thermal, emotional and perceptual assessments of a physical place may be intertwined with psychological schema-based and socio-cultural processes

findings.mechanism: Cultural differences in interpreting weather conditions, leading Swedes to perceive the weather as windier and colder.
findings.source: How do you perceive the weather today? section
findings.quote: compared to Japanese participants, Swedes estimated the current weather as significantly more windy, F(1,106)=15.10, P<.01 and colder, F(1,103)=5.57, P<.05.

findings.antecedent: Culture (Swedish vs. Japanese) AND Environmental attitude (urban vs. open-air)
findings.mechanism: Cultural and attitude-based differences in emotional response to place, resulting in Swedish urban persons feeling happier than Japanese urban persons.
findings.source: How do you feel right now in this place? section
findings.quote: A significant interaction between culture and attitude, F(1,104)=5.37, P<.05, showed that Swedish urban compared to open-air persons felt happier in the square, and that the opposite effect was observed for Japanese urban and open-air persons

findings.mechanism: Cultural differences in emotional response to place, leading Swedish participants to feel happier overall.
findings.source: How do you feel right now in this place? section
findings.quote: Finally, a main effect of culture showed that Swedish participants felt happier than Japanese participants, F(1,104)=5.26, P<.05

findings.mechanism: Cultural differences in emotional response to place, resulting in Swedish participants feeling significantly more calm.
findings.source: How do you feel right now in this place? section
findings.quote: two main effects of culture showed that Swedish participants felt significantly more calm being in the square compared to their Japanese counterparts [F(1,104)=5.07, P<.05]

findings.mechanism: Cultural differences in thermal perception and comfort, possibly linked to differing weather estimations, leading Swedes to feel more thermally comfortable.
findings.source: How do you feel right now in this place? section
findings.quote: as well as thermally more comfortable [F(1,105)=7.77, P<.01].

findings.mechanism: Cultural differences in thermal perception and comfort, leading Japanese participants to estimate weather as warmer and feel less thermally comfortable.
findings.source: How do you feel right now in this place? section
findings.quote: compared to Swedish participants the Japanese estimated the current weather as warmer and they felt less thermally comfortable (see Table 3) on the site
findings.empirical_support_cited: Beta=0.52, F=27.1, P=0.00 (for thermal comfort from cold/warm perception)

findings.mechanism: Cultural differences in aesthetic evaluation of place, leading Swedish participants to rate the square as more beautiful and pleasant.
findings.source: How do you perceive the place right now? section
findings.quote: compared to Japanese participants, Swedish participants estimated the square as significantly more beautiful [F(1,105)=8.03, P<.01]; and pleasant [F(1,105)=9.73, P<.01].

findings.mechanism: Cultural differences in perception of environmental conditions of the site, leading Swedish participants to perceive the square as windier and colder.
findings.source: How do you perceive the place right now? section
findings.quote: Furthermore, a two main effects analysis of culture showed that Swedish participants perceived the square as significantly more windy [F(1,105)=8.40, P<.01] (see Fig. 13) and colder, [F(1,105)=8.60, P<.01] (see Fig. 14) than did Japanese participants.

findings.mechanism: Mood influences aesthetic perception, where a positive mood leads to higher ratings of pleasantness.
findings.quote: This is in line with Gifford's (1980) result showing that persons in a positive mood compared to those in a less positive mood rated interiors as more pleasant.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Gifford (1980) result cited as supporting evidence.

findings.antecedent: Architectural design (Swedish square vs. Japanese square)
findings.mechanism: Different architectural styles/qualities might interact with cultural preferences and expectations, leading to divergent perceptual evaluations between cultures.
findings.quote: if we regard the Swedish square as architecturally more attractive than the Japanese square (see Figs. 1 and 2), then we may speculate that design per se may also have to some extent accounted for the cultural lack of correspondence in perceptual evaluation of the two squares.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Speculation based on visual comparison of the squares (Figs. 1 and 2) and observed cultural differences in perception.

findings.mechanism: Cultural norms, such as valuing modesty and avoiding extreme judgments, can lead to more conservative or lower self-reported environmental assessments, regardless of actual experience.
findings.quote: it must be noted that the differences in environmental assessments between Japanese and Swedish participants could in part reflect a 'cultural response bias', meaning that, compared to the Swedish participants, the Japanese might have evaluated the square, and how they felt while in the square, in a more modest way.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cited Eisler et al. (2003) on modesty as a valued personal attribute in Japan.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Persons living in different cultures with different environmental attitudes would psychologically evaluate a square differently despite similar thermal conditions.

Psychological as well as cultural influences will affect individuals' perceptions of a square despite a comfortable thermal environment, which, according to Mayer and Höppe (1987), should cause an equivalent thermal perception in participants.
bridge_warrants: The study connects thermal comfort research with psychological theories of perception (schemata) and socio-cultural influences, arguing that objective thermal indices alone are insufficient for predicting subjective experience.
It bridges the gap between physiological heat balance models and the role of cognitive and cultural factors in environmental assessment.
methodological_critiques: The quasi-experimental design means participants were not randomly assigned, potentially confounding independent variables with uncontrolled extraneous variables, thus weakening inferences about causal relationships compared to a true experiment.
model_structure: The paper implicitly proposes a model where objective physical environmental conditions (e.g., PET) are mediated by psychological (environmental attitude, schemata) and socio-cultural (culture, cultural norms) processes to produce subjective thermal, emotional, and perceptual assessments of a place. This model suggests a top-down influence of internal states and cultural priors on sensory interpretation.
limitations: Thermal comfort indices developed in line with physiological heat balance models may not be applicable in different cultural/climate zones without modifications.
Thermal comfort indices may not be appropriate if the psychological processes involved in environmental assessment are not taken into account.
The influence of cultural response bias (e.g., modesty in Japan) on environmental assessments is difficult to dissect given the data obtained.

paper_metadata.title: Emotional Responses to Multisensory Environmental Stimuli
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Emotional Responses to Multisensory Environmental Stimuli
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: How we perceive our environment affects the way we feel and behave. The impressions of our ambient environment are influenced by its entire spectrum of physical characteristics (e.g., luminosity, sound, scents, temperature) in a dynamic and interactive way. The ability to manipulate the sensory aspects of an environment such that people feel comfortable or exhibit a desired behavior is gaining interest and social relevance. Although much is known about the sensory effects of individual environmental characteristics, their combined effects are not a priori evident due to a wide range of non-linear interactions in the processing of sensory cues. As a result, it is currently not known how different environmental characteristics should be combined to effectively induce desired emotional and behavioral effects. To gain more insight into this matter, we performed a literature review on the emotional effects of multisensory stimulation. Although we found some interesting mechanisms, the outcome also reveals that empirical evidence is still scarce and haphazard. To stimulate further discussion and research, we propose a conceptual framework that describes how environmental interventions are likely to affect human emotional responses. This framework leads to some critical research questions that suggest opportunities for further investigation.
